Abstract (153 words) 20

Future changes in climate, demographic, and socioeconomic factors will deeply influence urban 21 building energy demand. We apply an integrated modeling approach to investigate the impacts 22 of the above drivers on building thermal energy service demand in 336 Chinese cities in 2020- 23 2060. We find that China’s urban building floor area will not decrease significantly due to 24 ongoing urbanization and increasing floor area per capita. However, future trajectories of 25 building thermal energy demand vary substantially across cities due to huge heterogeneity in 26 floor area and intensity of energy demand, suggesting the need for tailored infrastructure 27 planning and policy interventions. Future warming greatly changes demand patterns, reducing 28 heating demand by 24% but increasing cooling demand by 27% compared with no warming in 29 2060. Compact urban development and building energy efficiency improvements are key 30 demand-side measures, potentially reducing heating (cooling) demand in 2060 by 27% (24%) 31 and 22% (11%) relative to a scenario with limited policy interventions. 32

1. Introduction 37

Approximately 30% of global final energy consumption and CO2 emissions come from the 38 building sector 1. CO2 emissions from buildings have doubled over the past two decades and will 39 continue to grow under current policies 2. Therefore, future reductions in building energy use and 40 emissions will be crucial to global decarbonization. While electrification powered by clean 41 energy is regarded as an essential part of emission mitigation 3, measures that reduce energy 42 demand can make substantial contributions to the low-carbon transition of buildings as well 4–9. 43 Many studies have indicated that to achieve deep building decarbonization consistent with the 44 2 °C and 1.5°C climate targets, a portfolio of ambitious policies on both energy supply and 45 demand is necessary 10–16. 46

Effective reductions in energy use require a comprehensive understanding of future energy 47 demand and policy impacts. Previous literature has demonstrated that building energy use 48 changes as a function of various demand drivers, including climate 17–19, population size 14,18, 49 floor area per capita 14,20, energy behaviors 21, etc. These demand drivers have large geographic 50 variations, further complicating energy use patterns 22. In addition, policies on building energy 51 efficiency (e.g., building energy codes, old building retrofits) 7,11,23,24 and compact urban 52 development 25 also have great impacts on building characteristics and energy demand. The 53 natural, social, and policy factors collectively shape the future pathway of building energy 54 consumption and hence should be considered in demand projections. However, existing studies 55 rarely took these variations into account. Wang et al. (2023) 18 modelled the impacts of 56 population and climate on US building energy use at the city level, but they assumed fixed 57 building stock without including changes in floor area and building energy efficiency over time. 58

Chinese urban buildings are responsible for over 10% of China’s energy use and CO2 emissions 59

26, with more than half coming from space heating and cooling 27. As a result of rapid economic 60 development and urbanization, Chinese cities have witnessed sharp increases in building stock 61 and energy use over the past few decades. However, future energy use patterns of Chinese urban 62 buildings will be deeply influenced by changes such as a shrinking population 28, continued 63 urbanization 29, increasing floor area per capita due to income growth 27, improved energy 64 efficiency 11, and a warming climate 17. The future pathways of energy use and carbon emissions 65 of Chinese buildings have been extensively modelled at the national and climate zone levels 11,30– 66

36. Some studies provided city-level results, either using spatial downscaling 37 or with a limited 67 scope for one or several cities 17,38. Most studies failed to include the above demand drivers to 68 explore a wide range of scenarios, and they overlooked the inter-city heterogeneity in these 69 drivers. This lack of granularity limits the accuracy of energy and emission projections as well as 70 the ability to inform policymaking in individual cities. 71

To fill this research gap, here we evaluate the implications of future climate, demographic, and 74 socioeconomic changes for building thermal (heating and cooling) energy service demand in 336 75 Chinese cities from 2020 to 2060. We design a series of scenarios (Table 1) of the above demand 76 drivers and potential policies to model urban building energy demand in various possible futures. 77 We develop a bottom-up approach that includes the inter-city heterogeneity in building stock and 78 demand drivers for energy simulations. We estimate that China’s urban building floor area will 79 increase by 15% between 2020 and 2060 in the baseline scenario, due to continued urbanization 80 and increasing floor area per capita. We find huge inter-city heterogeneity in both building floor 81 area and thermal energy intensity. We find that climate, building energy efficiency, and floor 82 area per capita are primary drivers of energy demand. Future warming (Shared Socioeconomic 83 Pathway 245) is projected to result in changes in urban building heating, cooling, and total 84

thermal energy demand of -24%, +27%, and +8.5% in 2060, respectively. Ambitious policies on 85 compact urban development and building energy efficiency improvements could reduce national 86 urban building heating (cooling) demand by 22% (19%) and 8% (4%) from the baseline scenario 87 and by 27% (24%) and 22% (11%) from limited policy interventions (conservative policy 88 scenarios) in 2060, respectively. Policy impacts on building thermal demand vary substantially 89 across cities, suggesting that tailored infrastructure planning and policy interventions are needed 90 to effectively reduce energy use and emissions. 91

2. Materials and Methods 93

We integrate a modeling system to investigate the impacts of various energy demand drivers on 94 building heating and cooling demand from urban population in 336 Chinese prefecture-level 95 cities. First, we develop various scenarios of energy demand drivers by synthesizing projections 96 of future population, floor area, climate, as well as potential building policies. Second, we utilize 97 a building stock turnover model to project future building floor areas under these scenarios using 98 a historical urban building stock dataset. Next, we run a building energy use model to simulate 99 the heating and cooling energy intensities of prototype buildings in each city. Finally, we 100 combine the results of future city-level building stock and building energy intensities to evaluate 101 spatial and temporal variations in Chinese urban building energy demand. 102

2.1 Scenario design 103

We construct a series of scenarios to reflect the uncertainties in various drivers of urban building 104 stock and energy demand. We choose 2020 as the base year of our simulations and model the 105 pathways of city-level building energy demand from 2020 to 2060, when China pledges to 106 achieve carbon neutrality. 107

We build three urban population scenarios (HighPop, MedPop, LowPop) based on a dataset of 108 city-level population projections for China 28. The three scenarios assume national fertility rates 109 of 1.8, 1.3, and 0.7 by 2050, capturing a wide spectrum of possible population growth 110 trajectories based on recent trends and policies. As city-level urbanization rates are missing in 111 this dataset, we use the future provincial urbanization rates from Chen et al. (2020) 29 to estimate 112 urban populations and calibrate them against the urban population data from the 2020 China 113 Population Census. Figure S1 shows future changes in total and urban populations. Across the 114 three scenarios, China’s total population declines from 1.4 billion in 2020 to 1.1-1.3 billion in 115 2060. However, due to continued urbanization, China’s urban population will not decrease until 116 the 2040s, and the urban population in 2060 is comparable to or even higher than its 2020 value. 117

We develop three scenarios of building floor area per capita (HighArea, MedArea, LowArea) 118 based on empirical relationships between floor area and GDP from IEA (2015) 27 and projected 119


<!-- Page 6 -->


5

provincial GDP under the SSP2 scenario (consistent with the baseline climate scenario of this 120 study) from GCAM-China 40. We determine the residential floor area per capita of the 336 cities 121 in the base year (2020) based on the 2020 China Population Census, and we project different 122 future changes in city-level floor area per capita across the three scenarios (Figure S2). The 123 residential floor area per capita is averaged only over urban residents, given that urban and rural 124 residents of a city generally have different floor area per capita. China’s current floor area per 125 capita is still lower than many developed countries and is likely to increase with growing 126 resident income. In the MedArea and HighArea scenarios, the national average urban residential 127 floor area increases from 39 m2/capita in 2020 to 52 m2/capita and 56 m2/capita in 2060 128 (following historical patterns of global countries), respectively, due to economic growth and 129 uncontrolled expansion of urban lands. The LowArea scenario characterizes the potential effect 130 of ambitious compact urban development policy, where the national average building floor area 131 is limited to approximately 40 m2/capita (around base year level) through 2060. 132

In addition, we design three scenarios of future building energy efficiency (HighEff, MedEff, 133 LowEff). China has been promoting energy efficiency improvements for urban buildings by 134 upgrading the efficiency standards since 1986 17 and retrofitting old, inefficient buildings. As of 135 now, five generations of efficiency standards have been developed for residential buildings, and 136 three generations for non-residential buildings (Table S1). Here we assume a different pace of 137 efficiency improvements in the coming decades across scenarios. In the LowEff scenario, no 138 additional efficiency improvements will be implemented through 2060, and 0.18 billion m2 or 139 0.3% (current retrofit rate in China 39) of old buildings will be retrofitted per year through 2060, 140 representing existing policy efforts. In the MedEff and HighEff scenarios, we raise policy 141 ambitions by assuming the implementation of more stringent efficiency standards, where all new 142 buildings must meet the Nearly Zero Energy Building standards starting in 2035 and 2025. We 143 also assume more ambitious retrofits of old buildings in the MedEff and HighEff scenarios, with 144 a retrofit target of 0.39 billion m2 or 0.65% per year and 0.6 billion m2 or 1% per year (rate 145 consistent with China’s carbon neutrality goal by 2060 39) through 2060, respectively. These 146 policy impacts will vary across cities, as cities in different climate zones comply with different 147 standards, and cities differ in building vintage distribution as well. 148

Moreover, we include two climate scenarios (SSP245, SSP585) to evaluate the potential impacts 149 of climate change on future building energy use. In our main simulations, we use the SSP245 150 climate to construct a scenario with moderate warming. We also conduct sensitivity tests using 151 the SSP585 climate to assess the impacts of extreme warming on building energy demand. 152

We combine these four dimensions and generate 54 scenarios for building energy demand. We 153 use the MedPop_MedArea_MedEff_SSP245 scenario as the baseline scenario in this study. 154

2.2 Building stock turnover modeling 156

Modeling urban building energy demand requires information on building stock and its temporal 157

variations. However, no official sources in China provide consistent statistics on urban building 158

stock (e.g., building floor areas of residential and non-residential buildings) for all cities across 159

decades 41. Therefore, we use a dataset of historical Chinese city-level material stock 42 to 160

estimate the urban building floor areas of 336 cities from 1978 to 2020. We calculate the total 161

urban residential and non-residential building floor areas in each city and year by dividing the 162

material stock by material intensities for buildings. The building stock evolution before 1978 is 163

not considered, as the total urban building areas before 1978 are much smaller than their base 164

year values (and have mostly been replaced by 2020) and hence will not greatly affect our 165

analyses. As this dataset does not include vacant buildings, we adjust the building stock data 166

based on urban housing vacancy rates from the literature 43–45. 167

2.3 Future weather data 205

To include the effects of climate change on building energy demand, we extract future weather 206

data for the SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 207

Phase 6 (CMIP6) databases. We retrieve 6-hourly dry-bulb temperature, relative humidity, air 208

pressure, wind speed, and wind direction at the surface level of each city from a climate dataset 209

based on an ensemble of 18 CMIP6 models 49. Additionally, we retrieve 3-hourly global 210

horizontal irradiance and diffusive horizontal irradiance at the surface level of each city from the 211

Beijing Climate Center Climate System Model version 2 - Medium Resolution (BCC-CSM2- 212

MR) dataset 50. We calculate direct normal irradiance using global horizontal irradiance, diffuse 213

horizontal irradiance, and solar zenith angle 51. We use interpolation to convert these weather 214

variables into hourly data of dry-bulb temperature, dew point temperature, relative humidity, air 215

pressure, global horizontal radiation, direct normal radiation, diffuse horizontal radiation, wind 216

direction, and wind speed for building energy simulations. Given the interannual climate 217

variations in CMIP6 models, we use the 5-year average of weather variables as inputs for each 218

year of building energy simulation. 219

2.4 Building heating and cooling energy demand modeling 222

Urban building energy use can be modelled with top-down and bottom-up approaches. While 223 top-down models use aggregated data to characterize the relationship between building energy 224 use and its drivers, bottom-up models use disaggregated data to quantify the energy uses of 225 individual buildings and extrapolate them to the aggregated level 52. Here we take a bottom-up 226 approach, as we aim to investigate the impacts of future changes in climate and building energy 227 efficiency. 228

We employ a state-of-the-art building energy simulation model, EnergyPlus 229 (https://energyplus.net/), to simulate individual building energy intensities for heating and 230 cooling in Chinese cities. EnergyPlus is a physical model based on energy balance equations and 231 has been widely used for evaluating the response of building energy use to changes in climate 232 and building characteristics 18. As this study focuses on building energy demand drivers, we only 233 evaluate the final energy demand without explicitly modeling how the energy demand will be 234 met by different technologies. We design 92 prototype residential buildings (4 building types 235 (forms) × 5 climate zones × 3 or 5 building energy efficiency standards per climate zone) and 90 236 prototype non-residential buildings (6 building types (2 forms × 3 operation schedules (office, 237 mall, and hotel)) × 5 climate zones × 3 building energy efficiency standards) for Chinese cities 238 based on previous literature 17,53. We choose 5 years during 2020-2060 (2020, 2030, 2040, 2050, 239 2060) to conduct simulations. In combination, we perform a total of 127,680 EnergyPlus 240 simulations (336 cities × 38 prototype buildings per city × 5 years × 2 climate scenarios). We 241 assume a target temperature of 20°C for heating and 27°C for cooling for residential buildings 242 based on a Chinese indoor thermal comfort database 54. For non-residential buildings, we adopt 243 the heating and cooling patterns from China’s urban non-residential building energy efficiency 244 standards (Table S1). The model outputs are annual building heating and cooling energy uses at 245 an hourly resolution. 246

3. Results 285

3.1 Future urban building stock changes 286

We model future urban building stock changes in China at the city level based on projections of 287 urban population and floor area per capita (Section 4.1). Figure 1A-C show the national urban 288 building floor area changes from 1978 to 2060 in the baseline 289 (MedPop_MedArea_MedEff_SSP245) scenario. We estimate that the total urban building floor 290 area in 2020 (the base year of simulations) is 60 billion m2, with residential buildings making up 291 over 70% of the floor area. In the baseline scenario, while China’s total population began to 292 decline in 2020 (Figure S1), its urban population continues to increase until mid-century. 293 Building floor area grows until 2047, due to ongoing urbanization with associated population 294 increase and increasing floor area per capita. The total floor area in 2060 is 68 billion m2, 15% 295 higher than 2020, suggesting moderate potential for further building stock growth. New building 296 construction decreased significantly between 2020-2024 due to the real estate crisis in China 297 resulting from strict housing policies but is projected to recover afterwards due to recent policy 298 shifts promoting the real estate market. However, the future scale of building construction is 299 expected to be much lower than the peak during the 2010s (Figure 1B). 300

Future urban building stock varies substantially across different scenarios (Figure 1D). We find 301

that the total urban building floor area ranges from 50 billion m2 to 78 billion m2 in 2060, 302

depending on assumptions of population and floor area per capita. We note that only in scenarios 303

with compact urban development (the LowArea scenarios) would China stabilize the urban 304

building stock below the 2020 level in the coming decades. 305

In addition, in the baseline scenario, we examine changes in building vintage distribution over 306

time. Figure 1E, F show future urban building floor area by year of construction. We find that, 307

due to replacement of old buildings with new buildings that follow more stringent energy 308

efficiency standards, the share of buildings with relatively efficient envelopes increases rapidly 309

over time. In 2040, more than half of buildings will meet the energy efficiency standards in place 310

in 2020, and this share increases to 94% by 2060. The energy efficiency of new buildings built 311

after 2020 will largely determine the future energy demand of China’s urban buildings, 312

presenting a great opportunity to reduce future building energy demand through rapid 313

implementation of more stringent efficiency standards (e.g., the Nearly Zero Energy Building 314

Standard). 315

We find huge inter-city heterogeneity in the evolution of population and building floor area in 316

China for cities of various sizes (Figure S5). In the baseline scenario, while some cities witness a 317

decrease in urban population and building floor area over time, most cities (especially small 318

cities) will have a larger building stock by 2060. The changes in building floor area between 319

2020 and 2060 range from -80% to 200% across different cities. We observe similar patterns in 320

non-baseline scenarios. These huge variations in urban dynamics imply that policy priorities 321

regarding building energy and emission reductions should be contingent on the individual city 322

context. 323

3.2 Building heating and cooling energy intensities 324

We simulate building energy intensities for space heating and cooling services at the city level 325 under the SSP245 and SSP585 climate scenarios. 326

Heating and cooling energy intensities are dependent on multiple factors, including local climate, 327 building envelope energy efficiency, and building prototypes (e.g., height, floor plan, energy 328 behavior). Figure S6 and S7 illustrate the 2020 heating and cooling energy intensities of various 329 prototype residential and non-residential buildings of five representative cities in different 330 climate zones of China. We find substantial variations not only across cities but also across 331 different building vintages within a city. Building energy intensities are generally more sensitive 332 to efficiency upgrades in cities with a less temperate climate. In these cities, the heating and 333 cooling energy intensities of the most efficient buildings could be 60% lower than the least 334 efficient buildings. Our results demonstrate huge benefits of building efficiency improvements 335 for reducing energy demand. 336

In addition, we investigate the inter-city heterogeneity in building energy intensity due to 337

different local climate conditions. Figure S8A, B show the geographic variations in annual 338

heating and cooling intensities for the currently most efficient buildings (i.e., meeting the 2020s 339

standards) in 2020 under the SSP245 climate scenario. We observe high heating intensities in the 340

northeast and Tibet and high cooling intensities in southeastern cities. Warming under SSP245 341

results in a median reduction in heating energy intensities by 23% (25th-75th percentile: 15%- 342

31%) and a median increase in cooling energy intensities by 37% (25th-75th percentile: 26%- 343

51%) across different cities from 2020 to 2060. Cities with higher heating or cooling energy 344

intensities tend to experience larger changes in energy intensities over time (Figure S8C, D), 345

which indicates that the inter-city heterogeneity would decrease for heating while increase for 346

cooling as climate becomes warmer. Compared to the SSP245 scenario, the SSP585 climate 347

would further lower heating energy intensities (especially in central China) and increase cooling 348

energy intensities (especially in southern China) (Figure S8E, F). 349

3.4 Heterogeneous impacts of policies on cumulative urban building energy demand 415

We further estimate the cumulative building heating and cooling demand from 2020 to 2060 416 under various scenarios at the city level. We rank 336 Chinese cities by cumulative demand in 417 the baseline scenario and find that the top 50% of cities are responsible for 83% of national 418 urban building energy demand (Figure S17), with more than 25% of the national demand coming 419 from the top 20 cities. This concentrated pattern of building energy demand indicates the 420 importance of building policy implementations in these high-demand cities to overall demand 421 control. 422

We evaluate the geographic distribution of cumulative heating and cooling demand reductions 423 via increased efficiency and compact urban development (smaller floor areas). The differences 424 between the ambitious policy and limited policy scenarios of energy efficiency and floor area per 425 capita are shown in Figure 5. We find uneven impacts of these two policies across different 426 cities. Containing floor area growth has a larger impact on both heating and cooling demand in 427 most inland cities than coastal cities. This is because inland cities generally are less developed 428 and have lower floor area per capita than coastal cities in the base year (2020) and hence have 429 more potential for future floor area growth. In contrast, improving building envelope energy 430

4. Discussion 441

This study investigates the impacts of various demand drivers on Chinese urban building thermal 442 demand from 2020 to 2060 at the city level. We find that despite a shrinking population, 443 continued urbanization and increasing floor area per capita in the baseline scenario will result in 444 a 15% increase in total urban building floor area from 2020 to 2060. In addition, we find that 445 Chinese urban buildings will have higher cooling demand, lower heating demand, and higher 446 total energy demand (+8.5%) in 2060 due to a warming climate. China has pledged to peak 447 carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. Growing energy demand 448


<!-- Page 19 -->


18

increases the decarbonization challenge for the urban building sector and jeopardizes these 449 climate goals. Early, effective actions that contain floor area increases and improve building 450 energy efficiency are needed to avoid lock-in of future emissions associated with building 451 heating and cooling, reduce the demand for alternative energy sources, and accelerate the low- 452 carbon transition 55. 453

We demonstrate that building policies have great potential to lower energy demand via reducing 454 building floor area and enhancing building envelope energy efficiency. Ambitious policies on 455 compact urban development and efficiency improvements could reduce heating (cooling) 456 demand by 27% (24%) and 22% (11%) from the conservative policy scenarios in 2060. This 457 result is consistent with the finding of Güneralp et al. (2017) that, in developing countries, 458 promoting higher urban density is generally more effective in reducing building energy 459 consumption than efficiency improvements. Built-up area per capita is widely identified as an 460 important indicator of energy use and carbon emissions at both national and city levels 56,57. Our 461 analysis suggests that policymakers in China (particularly in fast-growing cities) should seize 462 this opportunity to contain floor area per capita by preventing excessive building construction. 463 However, we also note that the impacts of efficiency improvements may be underestimated, 464 since we only consider the building efficiency standards that are in effect or during the draft 465 stage. If China mandates more stringent efficiency standards before 2060, the resulting demand 466 reductions would be greater. 467

Our results reveal strong inter-city heterogeneity in building stock characteristics, energy 468 intensities, and energy demand, depending on the local patterns of population, floor area, and 469 climate changes. These variations imply that the portfolio of building decarbonization policies 470 should be tailored city by city to match the characteristics of future building energy demand. For 471 instance, for developed cities such as Beijing (Figure S15A, B) with decreasing population and 472 modest future floor area growth, the impacts of compact development might be limited. 473 Improving building energy efficiency could play a significant role in reducing Beijing’s heating 474 demand, while policies promoting energy saving practices can be adopted to contain the cooling 475 demand growth. In contrast, for growing cities such as Chengdu (Figure S15E, F), where rising 476 population and expanding floor area continue to drive energy demand, priority should be given 477 to compact development policies (e.g., limiting the construction of large-sized apartments). 478 Meanwhile, we find a highly uneven distribution of building energy demand among cities, with 479 half of the cities responsible for over 80% of energy demand. Targeting these high-demand cities 480 would provide most reductions in energy use and emissions, although eventually buildings from 481 all cities must be addressed to achieve net zero emissions. 482

Our results are subject to the following uncertainties and limitations. First, we analyze energy 483 service demand (demand for heating and cooling) rather than actual energy consumption (use of 484


<!-- Page 20 -->


19

electricity, gas, etc.), given the lack of city-level data on heating and cooling technologies. 485 Actual energy consumption of urban buildings will also depend on the technology mix and 486 efficiencies and is assessed in a national-level companion study (Liu et al., manuscript 487 submitted). Second, this study focuses on heating and cooling without accounting for other 488 building energy uses (e.g., lighting, cooking, and appliances). Unlike heating and cooling, other 489 energy demand will not be greatly affected by climate change but is expected to increase as the 490 economy grows. Third, we only model four types of residential buildings and six types of non- 491 residential buildings. In reality, there is a much higher diversity in building characteristics both 492 within and across different cities. Other building types (e.g., data centers) would show different 493 energy demand patterns and could be included by future studies. Fourth, as we take a bottom-up 494 approach by aggregating energy demand of individual buildings, urban climate factors (e.g., the 495 heat island effect) 58 are not included in the modeling. The exclusion of urban heat might result 496 in overestimated heating demand and underestimated cooling demand. 497

In conclusion, this study indicates that future climate, demographic, and socioeconomic changes 498 lead to large temporal and geographic variations in urban building thermal energy demand in 499 China. Tailored energy infrastructure planning and building policies in individual cities are 500 crucial to cope with this heterogeneity. Our findings suggest great opportunities for Chinese 501 cities to reduce building heating and cooling demand through policy interventions. 502
